In addition to proposing a commission structure for transactions on App Store external payment systems (IAP) outside the United States, Apple also filed a motion indicating its willingness to explore a settlement with Epic Games. Details below.

Apple may be prepared to settle with Epic

Earlier today, Apple submitted a proposal outlining the commission it hopes to collect on transactions completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

The timing of Apple's filing coincides with the Supreme Court's denial of Apple's request—Apple had sought to halt lower court proceedings while it appealed Judge Gonzalez Rogers' contempt ruling. Apple had previously been ordered to allow developers to redirect users to external payment methods, but was found in contempt after it continued to charge a 27% commission.

Under Apple's proposed structure, the company could collect up to a 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games immediately objected, claiming that it "believes these fees fall entirely outside the scope of guidance provided by the Ninth Circuit on permissible fees."

While this filing drew most of the attention, Apple also submitted another motion today, requesting Judge Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

Filing contents (edited for clarity):

This means Apple's legal team had contacted Epic's attorneys prior to filing the motion to discuss holding a settlement conference, but Epic did not agree to Apple's request.

Apple noted in its motion that the court has the authority to order both parties to attend a settlement conference even without Epic's consent, adding that the Ninth Circuit itself encourages both parties to reach agreement on an appropriate guided external link (link-out) commission.

The company also stated that "discussing potential settlement solutions in a confidential, non-adversarial environment would increase the likelihood of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding lengthy remand proceedings."

Notably, this filing does not include any settlement proposal or offer from Apple, nor does it constitute a settlement proposal in any meaningful sense. Apple is merely requesting that the court order settlement negotiations supervised by Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
